issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies an interpersonal/home-intrusion threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items, which center on contamination/body danger and intrusive sensory reliving.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' is not impossible after chemical exposure, but here it reads as preparation for assault/entrapment rather than avoidance of fumes, contamination, or bodily symptoms; it is weakly aligned with the rest of the profile and the trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus strongly on social/cultural disconnection and not belonging, which is difficult to reconcile as the central appraisal pattern for a 60-year-old male whose trauma was toxic chemical exposure. These appraisals are not impossible, but alongside the rest of the profile they are poorly connected to the main symptom pattern of somatic threat, false alarms, and sensory reliving. A clinician would question why chemically exposure-related PTSD is expressed mainly as community/cultural alienation rather than danger, contamination, mistrust of body, or permanent harm beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the profile is dominated by body-based threat and intrusive sensory memory, but the maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others' is not well supported because the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from all other nodes. Reminder-based avoidance centered on external prompts by others implies a trigger-driven maintenance pattern that is not reflected in the formulation or elsewhere in the self-report.

vignette: The valve had ruptured without warning, a sharp hiss followed by a thick, acrid cloud that rolled through the hotel's lower service corridors. Mateo Reyes had been coordinating a late-night pipe replacement when the safety seal failed. He remembered the way the air turned sharp against his tongue, a metallic bitterness that coated his throat and made him gag. He had coughed until his ribs ached, stumbling backward through the dimly lit utility tunnels, pressing his palm against the cool concrete walls while the ventilation system pulled the fumes deeper into the building. For forty minutes, he had waited for maintenance to override the pressure, trapped in a space where the air itself felt like a threat. When the doors finally opened, he had stepped out into the cool night air, but the metallic taste lingered long after he went home to wash his face. In the weeks that followed, Mateo's body refused to settle. He found himself pressing his palms to his chest each morning, running his fingers over his ribs, checking his skin for any new marks or rashes, as if a new exposure might be hiding beneath his clothes. His posture remained locked, shoulders drawn tight, muscles coiled as though he were still waiting for the next valve to fail. When a housekeeping cart rolled too slowly past the front desk, he would assume something was wrong, his breath catching until he saw the staff was simply sorting linens. He learned to leave staff meetings the moment someone mentioned industrial supplies or ventilation schedules, turning down conversations before they could begin. His girlfriend, Elena, had asked him twice if he felt his lungs were healing, and each time he had shifted the subject, certain that speaking about it would invite another wave of that suffocating weight. He had come to believe that he could not stop bad things from happening, and that he no longer belonged anywhere in his own routine. The memories did not arrive on schedule; they forced their way into his mind during quiet moments, usually in the parking garage when he was unlocking his car. The taste would return first, sharp and chemical, followed by the sensation that he was standing back in the service corridor, the hiss of the valve echoing in his ears as if it were happening right now. He would grip the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened, breathing through his mouth to keep the phantom taste from rising again. When maintenance trucks arrived late for scheduled checks, he would sit in his office with the blinds drawn, certain that another incident was already unfolding somewhere on the property. As hotel manager, Mateo spent his days moving through the very spaces that had once held him. He walked the guest corridors with his eyes fixed on the ceiling vents and the corners where service panels met the walls, counting exits and noting the hum of the HVAC units. Every time a fire alarm test chime sounded through the halls, his body would jolt, heart hammering, as though the threat were immediate and unavoidable. He avoided the maintenance wing entirely, delegating inspections to his assistant and taking his breaks in his office with the door closed. He missed the familiar cadence of Tagalog in the staff break room and the way his colleagues used to gather around his desk to share jokes, and the quiet distance between him and his work had grown palpable; he no longer felt like part of the staff he once led, as if he had stepped outside the boundaries of his own life. It was Elena who finally placed the appointment card on his nightstand. She had watched him flinch at the sound of a dripping faucet, notice him checking his pulse three times before dinner, and seen him stand in the kitchen doorway for minutes at a time, scanning the room as though looking for an escape route. He had finally agreed to go, not because he believed he could fix what had broken, but because he was exhausted from the constant vigilance. He told the intake specialist he was there because he no longer knew how to live in his own skin, afraid that if he stopped watching for danger, something worse would happen. He hoped, quietly, that he might learn to trust his body again, or at least find a place where he could stop waiting for the next valve to break.
